description_full: DuPont de Nemours, Inc. provides technology-based materials and solutions in the United States, Canada, the Asia Pacific, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. It operates through two segments, Healthcare & Water Technologies and Diversified Industrials. The company offers specialty components for medical devices, packaging and garments, and protective suits under the brand TYVEK; provides water filtration and separation solutions, including elements, modules, and systems serving primarily industrial wastewater and energy markets, municipal and desalination applications, and life sciences and specialty sectors. It also offers AMBERLITE ion exchange resins, FILMTEC reverse osmosis and nanofiltration elements, and INGE and ITEGRATEC ultrafiltration modules. In addition, the company offers engineered products and integrated solutions for the non-residential, residential, and repair-and-remodel construction markets, includes TYVEK house wrap, STYROFOAM insulation, and CORIAN solid surface. Further, it engages in the design and production of engineered components, systems, and process solutions used in OEM and operational applications, such as automotive, aerospace, printing, and packaging. Additionally, the company offers Vespel shapes and parts, MOLYKOTE specialty lubricants, BETAFORCE and BETASEAL structural adhesives, and Cyrel flexographic printing plates. The company has a collaboration with Microsoft and NobleAI to expand access to advanced AI tools and resources, including machine learning that helps scientists and engineers innovate faster. The company was formerly known as DowDuPont Inc. and changed its name to DuPont de Nemours, Inc. in June 2019. DuPont de Nemours, Inc. was incorporated in 2015 and is headquartered in Wilmington, Delaware.

financial_summary: DuPont de Nemours, Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $20.8B market cap on $6.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -19% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 22% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The business throws off $227M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 1.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.57x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 222 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 1.03, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $137.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 55% in the 2020 crash, 40% in the 2022 bear market and 85% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $107 (margin of safety -47%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 83%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $28.48 to $335 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 54.8 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 13.7 vs 7.9 and P/FCF 91.8 vs 21.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 474% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $172 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.24).
It runs a 22% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only -0.72x.
It spends 2.8% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.1x net debt to EBITDA ($715.0M of cash against $3.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 1.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.68 in the distress zone.
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -19.3% over 3 years and -19.6% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 31%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 3.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (4.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is -17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 9.6% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 82%.
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (1.5% in dividends, less 0.2% of net share issuance).
The share count has shrunk 10.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 53 consecutive years, though it has been cut 7.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 15,000 employees, each generates about $457K of revenue, 0.7x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has fallen 24.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $15K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (8x revenue per employee).
